Neonates of the Chinese giant salamander emerge from their gelatinous egg capsules after a developmental period of approximately 55 days [ab = approximately 55 days] when incubated at a stable water temperature of 14 °C [T = 14 °C]. At the moment of hatching, these aquatic larvae possess a modest total length of roughly 3 cm [Lb = roughly 3 cm] and exhibit a wet weight of merely 0.221 grams [Wwb = 0.221 grams], a figure derived from the average diameter of the heavily yolk-laden eggs which typically measure between 7 and 8 mm. The newly emerged larva remains entirely endotrophic during its initial days, subsisting entirely on the residual yolk reserves that sustain it before the onset of exogenous feeding. This lecithotrophic phase is critical, as the larva must develop functional gills and a rudimentary mouth structure before it can actively hunt for small aquatic invertebrates. The brief window of yolk dependence underscores a life-history strategy where early provisioning is concentrated into a dense packet of nutrients, allowing the embryo to achieve a relatively advanced developmental state by the time of eclosion. Field observations suggest that the duration of this embryonic period can vary slightly with minor thermal fluctuations, but the 55-day incubation benchmark provides a reliable reference for captive rearing protocols.

As the larvae progress through their aquatic tadpole stage, they undergo a prolonged period of somatic growth that, under the thermal conditions typical of their cool montane stream habitats (14 °C [T = 14 °C]), can extend for many years. During this phase, the animals are known to achieve an ultimate total length of approximately 150 cm [Li = approximately 150 cm] in the largest wild-caught specimens, a dimension that places them among the largest extant amphibians globally. The corresponding ultimate wet weight for such individuals can reach an astonishing 30,000 grams [Wwi = 30,000 grams], reflecting the robust, heavy-bodied morphology that characterizes this species. These impressive size records are typically observed in older, undisturbed populations occupying deep, well-oxygenated river systems with abundant crevice habitat. Growth rates are strongly influenced by food availability and water temperature; individuals in optimal conditions add considerable length and mass annually, while those in marginal habitats may plateau at far smaller asymptotic sizes. The sheer magnitude of these final dimensions imposes unique physiological demands, including an extremely low surface-area-to-volume ratio that necessitates cutaneous respiration across a highly wrinkled, vascularized skin.

Reproductive maturation in the Chinese giant salamander is a notably slow process, with individuals attaining sexual maturity and initiating their first reproductive event after approximately 5.5 years after hatching [tR = approximately 5.5 years after hatching] when maintained at a constant temperature of 14 °C [T = 14 °C]. This age at first reproduction is considerably later than in most smaller-bodied urodeles, a pattern consistent with the conservative life-history strategy typical of large, long-lived vertebrates. At the onset of breeding activity, males and females alike have typically reached a total length at puberty of around 45 cm [Lp = around 45 cm], with a documented natural range spanning from 40 to 50 cm depending on local resource conditions. The attainment of this critical body size appears to be a more reliable predictor of reproductive competence than chronological age per se, as individuals in resource-poor environments may require additional years to cross this size threshold. The extended juvenile phase allows for the accumulation of substantial somatic reserves, which are subsequently mobilized to support the considerable energetic demands of gamete production, nest guarding, and the prolonged period of paternal care that follows egg deposition.

The reproductive output of a gravid female Chinese giant salamander is characterized by a clutch of between 400 and 500 eggs [N_R_i = a clutch of between 400 and 500 eggs], deposited in a single annual event per breeding season under the cool thermal regime of 14 °C [T = 14 °C]. Females typically produce a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year], a modest frequency that reflects the substantial per-event investment required to manufacture such large, yolk-rich ova. This annual fecundity is relatively low for an amphibian of this size, but the strategic emphasis lies on the quality and protective environment afforded to each developing embryo rather than sheer numerical output. The male, who assumes exclusive guardianship of the egg mass after external fertilisation, fans oxygenated water over the developing embryonated eggs and aggressively defends them from predators, a behavior that significantly enhances hatching success rates. The combination of moderate egg number, extended parental care, and a late onset of reproduction is characteristic of a K-selected life-history strategy adapted to the stable, low-mortality environments of deep subterranean streams.

Longevity data for the Chinese giant salamander indicate that individuals can survive for up to 60 years [am = up to 60 years] under optimal captive conditions at a regulated temperature of 14 °C [T = 14 °C], making it one of the most long-lived of all amphibian species. This exceptional lifespan far exceeds that of most anurans and is matched only by a few other large, slow-growing urodeles, a pattern that correlates strongly with the species’ low metabolic rate and its occupation of a predator-scarce, thermally stable niche. The protracted maximum duration of life allows for multiple reproductive seasons, with experienced, larger females often producing larger clutches and more viable eggs than younger, first-time breeders. Senescence in this species is gradual, with no abrupt post-reproductive mortality; instead, individuals gradually lose physical condition over decades, eventually succumbing to disease, habitat degradation, or the cumulative effects of minor injuries sustained during territorial disputes. The 60-year benchmark, however, is seldom achieved in the wild due to anthropogenic pressures, including overharvesting for the luxury food trade and widespread habitat fragmentation that isolates populations.
